## The fin and its flow {#sec-basics}

### The fin and its section

The fin hangs below the hull and carries the lead bulb. Seen from the side it is a blade about 0.36 m
deep. Cut horizontally, every slice of it is a streamlined shape, the **section**
(@fig-fin-side, @fig-section). The simulations compute one such slice. They describe a fin with the
same section and chord all the way down, without its tip, bulb or hull junction.

[On a phone, pinch to zoom the diagrams, or turn the phone sideways.]{.mobile-hint}

![The fin seen from the side. The dashed line is the kind of horizontal slice the simulations
compute. Schematic, not to scale.](../_generated/fin-side.svg){#fig-fin-side width="300px"}

![That slice: NACA 0007 with a 100 mm chord, meeting the water at an angle of attack α. The side force
acts across the water flow and the drag along it. Schematic: the angle is exaggerated so it can be
seen.](../_generated/section.svg){#fig-section}

**Reading a name like "0007/100".** NACA 0007 is a symmetric section from the NACA four-digit family.
"00" means no camber: both sides have the same shape. "07" means its maximum thickness is 7\ % of the
chord. "/100" is the chord in millimetres. So 0007/100 is a section 100 mm long and 7 mm thick at its
thickest point, 30\ % of the chord back from the leading edge.

**Terms used on this page.** The symbols follow the project's
[nomenclature](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/nomenclature.md), which builds on
Parolini and Quarteroni [@parolini2007] and the ORC's VPP documentation [@orc-vpp2026].

* **Angle of attack α:** the angle between the section's chord line and the water it meets.
* **Leeway β~Y~:** the angle between where the boat points (its heading) and where it goes (its
  course through the water). The fin meets the water at this angle. In 3D, part of it is used up by the vortex at the fin's tip;
  the rest is the 2D section angle α that the simulations compute. At working load and 1 m/s that is
  about 4° of section angle plus about 1° for the tip. The comparisons only use differences between
  fins. At equal span and side force the tip part is the same for every fin, so a difference in α is a
  difference in leeway: Δβ~Y~ = Δα.
* **Side force S~h~ and drag D~h~:** the fin's share of the boat's hydrodynamic side force and drag.
  Their section coefficients C~l~ and C~d~ are the force per metre of span divided by q c, where
  q = ½ρV~b~² is the dynamic pressure, ρ the density of water, V~b~ the boat speed and c the chord.
* **Reynolds number** Re = V~b~ c / ν, with ν the kinematic viscosity of water (about 1.14×10⁻⁶ m²/s at
  15 °C). It sets how the boundary layer
  behaves. For 0007/100 at 1 m/s in water at 15 °C, Re ≈ 88,000. IOM fins work at 3×10⁴ to 2×10⁵.
* **Tu,** the turbulence of the incoming water: its random velocity fluctuations as a percentage of
  the speed. The simulations use 0.1\ % (calm) and 1\ % (more disturbed). Nobody has measured it on a
  model-yacht pond.
* **Flow-through:** the time the water takes to pass one chord, c / V~b~. For a 100 mm chord at 1 m/s
  that is 0.1 s.
* **Load** means the side force the fin must make, which the sails set: low, working and high load.
  **Wind** means the boat speed it brings: light air (about 0.75 m/s), medium (1 m/s) and fresh
  (1.5 m/s). That mapping is an assumption.

### The boundary layer, separation and bubbles

Right next to the surface the water is slowed by friction in a thin **boundary layer**.

* **A laminar boundary layer** flows in smooth sheets. Its friction is low, but it separates easily
  where the pressure rises towards the trailing edge.
* **A turbulent boundary layer** mixes. It has more friction, but it is more resistant to
  separation.

At IOM Reynolds numbers the layer starts laminar. On the suction side it often separates (S), turns
turbulent in the separated layer (T) and reattaches (R). The region between is a **laminar separation
bubble** (@fig-bubble), and its position and size decide much of the drag. The separated layer can
also roll up into vortices that are shed downstream (**vortex shedding**), fail to reattach at all at
low speed, or separate right at the leading edge at higher speed or angle. The videos and the gallery
in @sec-flows show each case.

![A laminar separation bubble, schematic. The laminar layer separates from the wall at S. The
separated layer (the line above the blue pocket) turns turbulent at T, away from the wall, and
reattaches to the wall at R. In the blue pocket the water next to the wall flows backwards. The small
arrows show velocity profiles, and the dashed line is the edge of the boundary layer. Not to
scale.](../_generated/bubble-schematic.svg){#fig-bubble}

### Where the drag comes from {#sec-drag}

The drag of an IOM fin, D~h~, has three main parts: skin friction D~f~, pressure drag D~p~ and
induced drag D~i~.

$$
D_h = \underbrace{D_f + D_p}_{D_v\text{, profile drag}} + D_i
$$

The first two together are called **profile drag**, D~v~ (the ORC's viscous drag): what the 2D section
simulations calculate. Induced drag comes from the fin's finite span.

#### 1. Skin-friction drag D~f~: water rubbing against the surface

Water touching the fin is stationary relative to it. Its speed rises through a thin boundary layer
until it reaches the speed of the surrounding flow. That velocity gradient creates friction.

* **Laminar flow:** orderly layers, relatively little mixing and low friction.
* **Turbulent flow:** mixing brings faster water towards the wall, increasing the velocity gradient
  and friction.

A smooth surface and less wetted area generally help. But keeping the boundary layer laminar is
beneficial only while separation remains under control.

#### 2. Pressure drag D~p~: pressure pushing back more than it pushes forward

Water accelerates around the front of the section, then slows as the pressure rises towards the
trailing edge. Ideally, much of that pressure recovers.

The slow water near the wall can struggle against this rising pressure and separate from the surface.
A separated region and wake can prevent effective pressure recovery, increasing drag.

**The important trade-off:** turbulent flow has more friction, but can reduce total drag by
preventing a much more costly separation.

At IOM fin Reynolds numbers, a laminar layer may separate, become turbulent, then reattach. This is a
laminar separation bubble (@fig-bubble). A short bubble can be relatively inexpensive; a long bubble
or separation without reattachment can be costly.

#### 3. Induced drag D~i~: the cost of producing side force

A real fin has a tip. Flow around it creates a trailing vortex system that changes the direction of
the local flow. Consequently, some of the fin's hydrodynamic force acts backwards.

Induced drag increases roughly with side force squared and decreases with span squared, with another
factor accounting for the lift distribution (the span efficiency e in
[From a section to a fin](#sec-section-to-fin)).

For these comparisons, fins have the same span and produce the same required side force. With the
same assumed span efficiency, their induced drag is therefore the same; it does not decide the
section ranking.

#### Which flow is desirable?

| Flow state | Drag consequence |
|---|---|
| Attached laminar boundary layer | Low friction and good pressure recovery: usually ideal. |
| Short separation bubble, then attached flow | Some additional loss, but potentially a good compromise. |
| Attached turbulent boundary layer | Higher friction, but often preferable to extensive separation. |
| Long bubble or open separation | Poor pressure recovery; often high drag. |
| Strong vortex shedding | Fluctuating forces; mean drag depends on the resulting separation and wake. |

: How the state of the boundary layer affects drag. The gallery (@sec-gallery) shows examples from
the simulations. {#tbl-flow-states}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Key takeaway.** The goal is not as little turbulence as possible. It is the lowest combined
friction and pressure drag while making the required side force. That is why calmer water
(@fig-flow-bubble-tu01), a thinner section, or an earlier transition can each help in one operating
condition and hurt in another.
:::

## Previous state of the art {#sec-prior}

::: {.callout-note}
## Scope of the evidence
* Class-rule figures come from the 2026 rules.
* Product figures are the makers' own claims, not measurements.
* Designers' views come from their articles and from forums, and are opinion.
* No published comparison of IOM fin sections in terms of race time was found.

Details and sources are in two research notes,
[iom-fins-on-the-market.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/iom-fins-on-the-market.md)
and [fin-stiffness.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/fin-stiffness.md).
Numbers on this page come from this project unless a source is cited.
:::

**Fins in use.** The class rules leave the fin almost free [@iom-rules-2026]:

* any material no denser than lead, so carbon is legal in the fin (though not in the hull);
* no minimum thickness, and at most 20 mm thick above the bottom 60 mm;
* a keel of 2.2–2.5 kg and a draft of 370–420 mm.

Every fin on the market with stated dimensions is a tapered carbon blade, about 80–100 mm in chord at
the hull and 63–75 mm at the bulb, 350–360 mm below the hull, 6–7\ % thick (about 5–6 mm).

* SAILSetc sells a 7\ % fin, 90 → 75 mm [@sailsetc-370iom].
* Craig Smith sells a 6\ % fin, 90 → 75 mm [@cs-cf1].
* Rob Nelson sells a fin of 100 → 70 mm, thickness not stated [@rn-gp].

No maker names its section. Graham Bantock's fins have used custom low-Reynolds-number sections by
David Hollom since 1992 [@hollom2008]. The designs winning world championships (V12, VISS, Venti, K2)
come with their own fins, whose dimensions aren't published [@iomica-hof]. Designers agree that thin
is fast: "the thinnest is best, around 6\ %", with a longer chord if the fin needs strength
(Bantock, as recalled in a forum). Proposals for a minimum fin thickness were defeated in the 1990s
[@bantock-iom1]. The typical leeway in the No. 1 rig is about 3° [@gilbert-finforce]. *Not found:*
any published comparison of fin sections or chords for IOMs in terms of race time.

**Low-Reynolds-number aerofoils.** Wind-tunnel polars at Re ≈ 10⁵ [@selig1989] show how laminar
separation bubbles set the drag of thin sections. This project checks its model against those polars
(@sec-validation).

**Predicting transition.** RANS turbulence models can be combined with a transition model
[@menter1994; @langtry2009]. Their known weak spot is separation bubbles.

**Surface finish and trips.** Roughness on model yachts is covered by @klaka2022, and
boundary-layer trips on low-Reynolds-number aerofoils by @lyon1997. The project's research note
[surface-roughness.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/surface-roughness.md)
has the details.

**Fin stiffness.** It matters mainly for holding the bulb, by limiting sag at high heel and
oscillation in waves. Its value in race time hasn't been measured (@sec-conclusion).

**What this project adds:**

* a ranking by race time rather than drag coefficient, with leeway and the downwind leg counted;
* a check of the steady solutions against time-accurate ones;
* the ranking at three boat speeds.

## Methodology {#sec-method}

### Simulating a fin section

Each simulation is a 2D slice of the fin: one section at one angle of attack and one boat speed, in
fresh water at 15 °C. It uses OpenFOAM v2512 [@openfoam] with the k-ω SST turbulence model
[@menter1994] and the γ-Re~θ~ transition model of Langtry and Menter [@langtry2009]. The transition
model predicts where the boundary layer stays laminar, separates, reattaches or turns turbulent. At
these Reynolds numbers that decides most of the drag. It needs Tu as an input.

Two solvers are used:

* **Steady** (simpleFoam) finds a flow that doesn't change in time. It is cheap enough to sweep
  hundreds of cases per run, but where the real flow is unsteady its answer can be wrong
  (@sec-transient).
* **Time-accurate** (pimpleFoam) follows the flow in time, here for 30 flow-throughs. The forces are
  averaged over the last 6. It costs 8–13 hours per case on one core.

The mesh (@fig-mesh) is a structured C-grid written directly by the project's own generator: 90,112
hexahedral cells, wall-normal grid lines, the first cell sized for y⁺ ≈ 0.5 so that the viscous
sublayer is resolved, and a far field 50 chords away. Doubling the cell count changes drag by 0.1–0.2\ %
at 4° and 0.8–1.7\ % at 6°, and lift by under 0.4\ % (study `mesh-finalists`).

![The medium C-grid for NACA 0007 at 100 mm chord: the whole domain (every 4th grid line), the
section, and the leading edge. Drawn by the same code that writes the simulation
mesh.](../_generated/mesh.png){#fig-mesh}

### Validation {#sec-validation}

The model was checked on one section, NACA 0009 at Re = 10⁵, against wind-tunnel data from Princeton
[@selig1989]:

![NACA 0009 at Re 10⁵, coarse mesh, Tu 0.1\ %, steady solver. The transition model (used for every
result on this page) gets lift within 6\ % up to 8°. Drag is 10\ % high at 4° and 25\ % high at 8°, where
a laminar separation bubble dominates. The fully turbulent model has too much drag at low angles
because it misses the laminar flow.](../_generated/validation.svg){#fig-validation}

This supports using the model in this regime: thin symmetric sections at Re around 10⁵ and small
angles. It does **not** show that the model ranks sections correctly when they differ by less than
1\ % of race time. The ranking assumes the model's errors are similar for similar sections, and no
measurement here confirms that. Absolute drag is uncertain by roughly 10–25\ %. Likely causes, roughly
in order:

1. the transition model's handling of separation bubbles;
2. the tunnel's effective turbulence;
3. steady solutions of an unsteady flow at 4°;
4. mesh resolution;
5. scatter in the experiment itself.

### From a section to a fin {#sec-section-to-fin}

Each simulation gives a lift and drag coefficient, C~l~ and C~d~. They are scaled to the whole fin's
side force S~h~ and drag D~h~, with span b = 0.36 m below the hull, chord c and dynamic pressure q:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_h &= C_l\, q\, c\, b \\
D_h &= \underbrace{C_d\, q\, c\, b}_{D_v} + \underbrace{\frac{S_h^2}{2\pi\, q\, e\, b^2}}_{D_i}
\end{aligned}
$$

D~v~ is the section's profile drag. D~i~ is the induced drag of the tip vortex, from lifting-line theory
with the hull as a reflection plane and span efficiency e = 0.9. All fins have the same span, so at equal side force
their induced drag is the same: it adds to the total but doesn't reorder the fins.

### Compare at equal side force

The sails decide how much side force the fin must make, not the fin. So every fin is compared at the
same three side forces, the **loads**: what one reference section (0009/80) makes at 2°, 4° and 6°. At
1 m/s these are 1.15 N (low load), 6.69 N (working load) and 8.33 N (high load). These are loads, not
wind strengths. For each fin, interpolating along its lift curve gives the angle it needs, and along
its drag curve its drag, at that force (@fig-equal-force).

![The two steps of the comparison at 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, for the four best fins. Left: the angle each
fin needs to make each load. Right: its drag at that load. Diamonds are time-accurate points that
replaced steady ones (dashed). The steady points overestimated lift, so every fin needs more angle
than the steady curves suggested.](../_generated/equal-force.svg){#fig-equal-force}

A longer chord makes the same force at a lower angle, and so with less leeway.

### Race time

Upwind there are two costs, and downwind one (@fig-course):

![Upwind, the boat heads 39° off the true wind [@gilbert-vmg] and slides about 3° sideways (leeway
β~Y~), so its course is at β~TW~ = 42° to the true wind [@gilbert-finforce]. Downwind the fin makes no side force and meets the water at
0°.](../_generated/course.svg){#fig-course}

* **Drag slows the boat.** Extra drag ΔD~h~ costs a fraction of the leg's time of
  $$\text{drag loss} = \frac{\Delta D_h}{V_b\,\mathrm{d}D_h/\mathrm{d}V_b},$$
  where dD~h~/dV~b~ is the slope of the boat's total hydrodynamic drag (its resistance) with boat
  speed. V~b~ dD~h~/dV~b~ ≈ 1.35 N at 1 m/s,
  estimated from hull, fin, bulb and rudder friction. At that slope 0.01 N of extra drag costs 0.74\ %
  of the leg.
* **Leeway lengthens the path.** Sailing a distance d to windward takes d / cos β~TW~ of sailing,
  where β~TW~ = 42° is the true wind angle measured from the course. One more degree of leeway costs
  tan β~TW~ · Δβ~Y~ ≈ **1.57\ %** of the leg. The difference in
  leeway between two fins is the difference in their 2D section angles, because the tip-vortex part is
  the same at equal span and side force.
* **Downwind** the fin's drag at 0° counts, at the same boat speed.

With equal time upwind and downwind, a fin's loss is half the sum of the three. It is measured against
the best fin at each load and averaged over the three loads.

**Reading "×1 / ×2".** The resistance slope is the least certain input, so every result is computed
twice: with the estimated slope (×1) and with it doubled (×2). Tables show both as "×1 / ×2". It is a
sensitivity check on one input, not an error bar.

An example at working load: 0008/90 is 0.92\ % behind 0007/100. Its extra upwind drag (0.016 N) costs
0.60\ %, its extra 0.36° of leeway 0.29\ %, and its extra downwind drag 0.03\ %. The full method is in
[methodology.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/projects/foil2d/methodology.md).

The course angle uses a typical leeway of 3° [@gilbert-finforce]. The simulations imply about 5° at
working load: 4° of section angle plus about 1° for the tip vortex. With 5°, each degree of leeway
would cost about 7\ % more, which would favour longer chords slightly (an estimate; not included).

### Robustness

A fin can win on average and still lose badly somewhere. So the ranking is repeated for each boat speed
(0.75, 1 and 1.5 m/s) and each combination of:

* water turbulence (Tu 0.1\ % and 1\ %);
* resistance slope (×1 and ×2);
* solver (steady or time-accurate points).

A fin's **regret** in each case is how far it is behind the best fin there. The largest regret says
how badly the choice could turn out.

## Results {#sec-results}

Click any chart to see it larger.

### Steady and time-accurate {#sec-transient}

The steady solver's 4° solutions for the most promising thin sections never settled: their drag
oscillated by up to 22\ %. Time-accurate runs showed why: the flow itself is unsteady. At 4° the flow
shed vortices:

* in all the cases tested at 1 m/s (seven sections);
* in all the cases tested at 0.75 m/s (four sections);
* in all four at 1.5 m/s, NACA 0007/100 when started from rest, and in 0007/100 at 1.25 m/s.

Started from its steady solution, 0007/100 at 1.5 m/s ends in a different flow instead
(@sec-by-speed).

Getting a reliable time average took two lessons (@fig-force-history):

* **An impulsive start leaves a slow lift build-up.** Lift approaches its final value as the Wagner
  function predicts [@wagner1925; @jones1938]: about 95\ % after 15 flow-throughs, 99\ % after 30. The
  first runs stopped at 15 and were still drifting. They were continued to 30 from where they stopped.
* **Starting from the steady solution settles in about 10 flow-throughs.** The mean is the same either
  way.

![Lift at 4° and 1 m/s. Left: 0007/100 started from rest, continued at 15 flow-throughs; the
dash-dot line is the Wagner build-up scaled to the final mean. Right: 0009/100 started from the steady
solution. Thin lines are the instantaneous lift, which oscillates by about 10\ % as vortices are shed;
the forces are averaged over flow-throughs 24–30 (shaded).](../_generated/force-history.svg){#fig-force-history}

The settled means are checked by comparing the two halves of the averaging window: they agree to
within 1.3\ %. Halving the time step changes lift and drag by about 1\ %.

![Lift and drag coefficients at 4° and 1 m/s, steady against time-accurate. Every section tested makes about
the same time-accurate lift, C~l~ 0.39–0.40. The steady solver spread them from 0.41 to 0.47, and the
thick sections were the most wrong.](../_generated/steady-vs-transient.svg){#fig-steady-vs-transient}

**What changed, by angle:**

* **At 6°** (checked at 1 m/s) the flow is steady, but the steady drag was still 4–6\ % high for the
  0007 and 0008 sections (within 0.5\ % for 0009).
* **At 4°** (0.75, 1 and 1.5 m/s) the steady points were too optimistic about lift and too pessimistic
  about drag, and not by the same amount for every section. That reordered the fins.
* **At 2°** (1 m/s) the 0008 sections, which looked perfectly steady in the steady solver, shed
  strongly.

### The ranking at 1 m/s

For each side-force load, a fin's loss is measured against the best fin at that load; the mean
averages the three loads. Different fins win different loads, so even the best mean is above zero.

rest. Less is better.](../_generated/race-time.svg){#fig-race-time}

**One fin for every wind, with one open question.**

* **At 0.75 and 1 m/s:** NACA 0007/100 is best, by about 0.5\ % of race time (2 boat lengths per
  race).
* **At 1.5 m/s:** 0007/100 and 0008/100 tie. 0007/100 is 0.09\ % ahead with the estimated resistance
  slope, and 0.05\ % behind with it doubled.

**The open question: two flows at 1.5 m/s.** The model finds two different flows on 0007/100 at
1.5 m/s (@fig-leading-edge-bubble). Both start with a short separation near the leading edge. They
differ in what follows:

* **Started from rest,** the flow behind it rolls up into vortices that travel along the rear half,
  as on every other section. C~d~ is 0.0124–0.0125 in two simulations with different time steps. It
  does the same at 1.25 m/s.
* **Started from its steady solution,** it reattaches as a turbulent boundary layer and stays
  attached to the trailing edge. That has about 40\ % more friction and 22\ % more drag (C~d~
  0.0152).

Which flow a fin on a boat gets is not known. A boat reaches 1.5 m/s by accelerating through the
shedding flow, which argues for the first, but that has not been tested. If the second is real,
0007/100 is last of the four at 1.5 m/s, 1\ % (about 4 boat lengths) behind 0008/100. The same
leading-edge mechanism made the thinnest section, NACA 0006, lose at working load in selection run 2.

![NACA 0007/100 at 4° and 1.5 m/s: the two flows the model finds. Pressure and skin friction on the
suction side. Green: started from rest, one instant of a time-accurate run; the friction swings as
vortices pass. Red: started from its steady solution, where the flow settles and stays steady.
Negative skin friction is reversed flow.](../_generated/leading-edge-bubble.svg){#fig-leading-edge-bubble}

## How the water flows {#sec-flows}

The videos and pictures below are all from the 2D simulations.

* The water flows from **left to right**.
* The **suction side**, where the bubbles form, is on top.
* Each one says what its colours mean, because they differ.

### Vortex shedding, seen three ways

The three videos show the same run: NACA 0007/100 at 4°, 1 m/s (Re 88,000), Tu 0.1\ %,
time-accurate on the medium mesh.

* **Length:** 0.3 s of real time (3 flow-throughs, 150 snapshots), slowed about 34 times.
* **What happens:** the laminar boundary layer on the top surface separates and rolls up into
  vortices, which travel over the rear half and into the wake. About 13 pass in 0.3 s, around 40–45 a
  second.
* **Effect on lift:** it fluctuates by about 10\ % of its mean as they pass.

#### 1. Flow speed

**Colour:** the speed of the water relative to the free stream (speed / V~b~), whatever its direction.

* dark blue: nearly still;
* green: about 0.6;
* yellow to olive: about the free-stream speed;
* red: up to 1.6 times the free-stream speed, over the front of the suction side.

Dark blue means slow, not necessarily backwards. **Black lines** are streamlines.

**Look for:** the slow layer on the top surface thickening towards the back and wobbling as vortices
pass, and the wake behind the trailing edge waving up and down.

::: {#fig-shedding}
{{< video ../assets/shedding-velocity.mp4 >}}

Flow speed and streamlines around NACA 0007/100 at 4° and 1 m/s.
:::

#### 2. Reversed flow along the surface

**Colour:** the velocity along the surface direction, signed, relative to the free stream.

* pale: the free stream;
* amber: faster than it;
* dark grey: nearly still;
* blue: water flowing **backwards**, towards the leading edge.

**Look for:** blue pockets that form around mid-chord and roll back to the trailing edge. Each is a
vortex with backflow under it.

::: {#fig-shedding-boundary-layer}
{{< video ../assets/shedding-boundary-layer.mp4 >}}

The same run, close to the suction side: blue is reversed flow.
:::

#### 3. Spin (vorticity)

**Colour:** how fast the water spins (vorticity ω, scaled as ω c / V~b~).

* blue: clockwise, as seen here;
* red: anticlockwise;
* grey: no spin.

The top surface's boundary layer spins clockwise (blue) and the bottom's anticlockwise (red).

**Look for:** the blue layer on top rolling up into separate blobs near the back. Behind the trailing
edge, blobs of both colours alternate: a vortex street.

::: {#fig-shedding-vorticity}
{{< video ../assets/shedding-vorticity.mp4 >}}

The same run as vorticity.
:::

### How the flow changes with angle

**Colours** as in video 2:

* pale: the free stream;
* dark: slow water near the wall;
* blue: reversed flow.

**Look for** the blue region moving forward as the angle rises.

::: {#fig-angle-sweep}
{{< video ../assets/flow-angle-sweep.mp4 >}}

NACA 0009/80, 1 m/s, Tu 1\ %, steady solutions at 0°, 2°, 4°, 6° and 8°, one frame per angle.

* **0–2°:** the flow separates only near the trailing edge.
* **4°:** a bubble at mid-chord, from 28\ % to 69\ % of the chord, that reattaches.
* **6–8°:** a short bubble at the leading edge, with turbulent flow behind it.

Drag rises from C~d~ 0.014 to 0.040.
:::

### A gallery of flows {#sec-gallery}

Each picture is the suction side of one simulation (@fig-bubble explains the terms).

**Colours** as in video 2:

* pale: the free stream;
* amber: faster than the free stream;
* dark: the slow layer next to the wall (the boundary layer);
* blue: flow going backwards.

Pictures from time-accurate runs show a single instant. Captions give the section and chord, the
angle, the boat speed, the water turbulence (Tu) and the solver.

**Healthy: attached flow.**

attached over most of the chord. The flow reverses only near the trailing edge, from about 69\ % of the

**A laminar separation bubble, and what calm water does to it.**

![NACA 0009, 80 mm, 4°, 1 m/s, Tu 1\ %, steady. The laminar boundary layer separates at 28\ % of the
chord, turns turbulent in the separated layer and reattaches at 69\ %: a laminar separation bubble.
C~d~ 0.0164.](../assets/flow-bubble-tu1.png){#fig-flow-bubble-tu1}

![The same section in calmer water (Tu 0.1\ %). The bubble starts earlier, at 16\ %, and the flow
separates again from 54\ % to the trailing edge. Drag is 14\ % higher (C~d~ 0.0187). Calm water delays
the turbulence that closes the bubble, so it is not faster.](../assets/flow-bubble-tu01.png){#fig-flow-bubble-tu01}

**Vortex shedding.**

![NACA 0007, 100 mm, 4°, 0.75 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, time-accurate, one instant. The separated layer doesn't

Lift fluctuates by about 10\ % of its mean.](../assets/flow-shedding.png){#fig-flow-shedding}

![The same instant as vorticity (the spin of the flow). The shear layer on the suction side (blue)
rolls up into vortices, which leave the trailing edge as a wake of alternating

**Irregular shedding at a small angle.**

![NACA 0008, 100 mm, 2°, 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, time-accurate, one instant (vorticity). Near the trailing

had not settled after 20 flow-throughs. The steady solver showed a smooth, steady flow
here.](../assets/flow-irregular-2deg.png){#fig-flow-irregular-2deg}

**A leading-edge bubble, then turbulent flow.**

![NACA 0006, 80 mm, 4°, 1 m/s, Tu 1\ %, steady. The thinnest section separates right at the leading

![NACA 0009, 80 mm, 4°, 0.25 m/s (Re 17,600), Tu 1\ %, steady. At very low speed the separated laminar

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

*Everything here comes from a 2D model of the fin section, not from tests of a finished fin. The checks
the answer was waiting for are done. Confidence in it is medium, for the reasons under "Why the order
is not certain" below.*

**One fin for every wind: NACA 0007/100.**

* **Light and medium air (0.75–1 m/s boat speed): NACA 0007/100.**
  * It is about 0.5\ % of race time (2 boat lengths per race) ahead of the next best, 0007/90.
  * It is 0.7–0.8\ % (3 boat lengths) ahead of 0008/100.
* **Fresh air (1.5 m/s boat speed): NACA 0007/100 and 0008/100 tie,** within 0.1\ %.
  * That holds for the flow the model finds when started from rest.
  * If the higher-drag flow it finds from a steady start is the real one, 0008/100 is about 1\ %
    (4 boat lengths) ahead in fresh air (@fig-leading-edge-bubble).

Few sailors change fins with the wind, so the question is what one fin for every wind gives away
(@tbl-fin-choice).

[Scroll the table sideways →]{.table-hint}

::: {#tbl-fin-choice}
{{< include ../_generated/fin-choice.md >}}

What each fin gives away at each wind against the best fin there: the one with the smallest averaged
loss at that speed, which you'd fit if you could change fins. % of race time, ×1 / ×2 (estimated
resistance slope / doubled).

* **Assumptions behind "average":** half the race time upwind and half downwind, the three side-force
  loads weighted equally at each speed, and the three boat speeds weighted equally.
* **Boat lengths:** about 4 per 1\ % over 2 laps of 90 m legs (an estimate).
:::

**Best all-round: NACA 0007/100**, on current evidence.

* **It is the best, or within 0.05\ % of the best, in every wind.**
  * Against changing fins with the wind it gives away 0.00\ % of race time on average (0.02\ % with
    the resistance slope doubled), under 0.1 boat lengths per race.
  * That assumes 2 laps of 90 m legs, half the time upwind and half downwind, and equal weight for
    the three loads and the three boat speeds.
  * 0007/90 gives away 0.45\ % and 0008/100 0.52\ %.
* **If the higher-drag fresh-air flow is real,** it gives away 0.33\ % (about 1.4 boat lengths), all
  in fresh air. It is still the best all-round fin then.
* **0007/90 is the most even:** never more than 0.55\ % behind. But it is the least stiff of the
  three.

**Stiffness.** At IOM speeds the bulb loads the fin more than the water does: at a heel φ of 30° the part of
a 2.4 kg bulb's weight across the fin is about 12\ N, against about 7\ N of side force S~h~. A soft fin
lets the bulb sag to leeward at high heel, which costs righting moment RM~φ~, and lets fin and bulb oscillate in
waves. One designer describes a boat (a Ten Rater, a larger radio class) that "would slow and spurt
unpredictably in waves" until a stiffer fin was fitted [@gilbert-finpos]. Nobody has published how much stiffness is worth in race time, and the
leading designers put thinness first, getting stiffness from the chord and the layup. A fin's bending
stiffness scales roughly with chord × thickness³, so at 100 mm NACA 0007 is about 50\ % stiffer at the
root than a 7\ % fin with a 90 mm chord, and NACA 0008 at 100 mm is another 30–50\ % stiffer (estimates
for the same construction). Stiffness doesn't rule out 0007/100; if the boat sails a lot in waves at
high heel, or the bulb sits well aft of the fin, 0008/100 is the safer side. The details and the
sources are in the research note
[fin-stiffness.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/fin-stiffness.md).

**How much is at stake.**

* **Changing fins with the wind:** nothing gained with the flow found from rest. If the
  higher-drag fresh-air flow is real, up to about 1\ % of race time (4 boat lengths) in fresh air.
* **0007/100 against the next best fin:** 0.45\ % of race time on average with the estimated
  resistance slope (about 2 boat lengths), 0.24\ % with it doubled.

These are smaller than the uncertainties of the 2D model (@sec-validation). By comparison, sanding
finer than 400–600 grit gains less than half a boat length, but a dirty, slimy or unfair hull can cost
as much as a poor section choice or more [@klaka2022]. Choose the section, *and* keep the boat clean
and fair.

**Why the order is not certain:**

* **The model.** It is checked against one section at one Reynolds number (@sec-validation). It isn't
  validated for ranking sections that differ by under 1\ %, and the shedding hasn't been compared with
  measurements.
* **Two flows in fresh air.** The model finds two flows on 0007/100 at 1.5 m/s, and which one a
  real fin gets is not known.
* **Not every point is time-accurate.** At 0.75 and 1.5 m/s only the 4° points are; 0.5 m/s has none.
* **2D, constant chord.** Tip, bulb, hull junction, heel and taper are not modelled.
* **Estimated inputs.** The resistance slope and the water turbulence are estimates. The hull and
  rudder are assumed to make no side force, and every wind is weighted equally.

**Against what is sold.** The recommended thickness, 7\ %, is what the market sells and what designers
recommend. The chord is not: the simulations favour 90–100 mm, because a longer chord needs less leeway,
while commercial fins taper from 80–100 mm at the hull to 63–75 mm at the bulb (a mean of about
75–85 mm). The 2D model can't weigh taper, which moves lift and bending moment towards the root and
saves weight at the tip. In practice, "NACA 0007 at 100 mm" means a 7\ % fin at the long end of what is
sold; a 3D comparison of a tapered fin is the open question.

**What would change it:**

* a test of which flow a moving fin gets at 1.5 m/s: in the simulation, the speed ramped up from
  1.25 m/s; on the water, a trip strip that fixes where the boundary layer turns turbulent;
* a hull resistance curve, to replace the estimate;
* a 3D check of 0007/100 against 0008/100, and of a tapered 7\ % fin (for example 100 → 70 mm) against
  a constant 100 mm chord;
* a bench test of a real fin's stiffness: the tip drop with the keel held horizontal and the bulb on.

## How the work went {#sec-studies}

The work went in small steps, each a study with a question; its answer set up the next one. Each study
has a dated findings log in the repository.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The studies, one by one (click to open)

::: {#tbl-studies}
| when | study | question | answer |
|:----|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------------|
| 11\ Oct | validation | Does the transition model match wind-tunnel data at Re 10⁵? | Lift within 6\ %, drag 10–25\ % high, for this one section: it supports the model at Re 10⁵ (@sec-validation). |
| 12\ Oct | selection run 1: 0006, 0009, 0012 × 80, 100 mm; 360 cases | How do thickness and chord trade off? | A thin, short fin wins at low load and a longer chord at high load. At working load the optimum lies between 6\ % and 9\ % thick. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 2: 0006–0012 × 80, 90, 100 mm; 450 cases | Where between 6\ % and 9\ %? | Thin sections lose at working load because their laminar boundary layer separates at the leading edge. NACA 0012 is out. |
| 13\ Oct | mesh check | Is the mesh fine enough to separate the finalists? | Yes: medium is within 0.2\ % of fine at 4°. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 3: four finalists at Tu 0.1\ %; 100 cases | Does calmer water change the order? | Calmer water means *more* drag at 4–8°: the laminar bubble grows. |
| 13\ Oct | analysis: leeway and both legs | What does the drag difference cost on the race course? | Counting leeway favours longer chords again; 0008/90 looked like the safest all-rounder. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 4: 0007/90, 0007/100, 0008/100; 75 cases | Are the thinner, longer sections better still? | Possibly, but the steady 4° solutions oscillated too much to tell. |
| 14\ Oct | time-accurate check 1: 10 cases | Are the oscillating steady points right? | At 6° yes for the 0009 sections, within 0.5\ %. At 4° all seven sections shed vortices at 1 m/s, and 15 flow-throughs were too few to settle. |
| 15\ Oct | time-accurate check 2: 8 cases continued to 30 flow-throughs | Where do the 4° forces settle? | Lift 4–16\ % below steady. 0007/100 moves to first, 0008/90 to fourth. |
| 17\ Oct | time-accurate check 3: the top four at 2° and 6°, and at 0.75 and 1.5 m/s; 15 of 16 cases | Does that hold at other angles and speeds? | At 0.75 and 1 m/s, yes. At 1.5 m/s 0007/100 switches to a leading-edge bubble and drops to last of the four. The steady 6° drag of the 0007 and 0008 sections was 4–6\ % high. |
| 17\ Oct | time-accurate check 4: 0007/100 at 1.5 and 1.25 m/s, started from rest; 1 of 2 cases | Is that 1.5 m/s result real? | From rest it sheds, with 18\ % less drag: the high-drag flow came from the steady start. The 1.25 m/s case blew up. |
| 18\ Oct | time-accurate check 5: the same two at half the time step | Does it hold, and at 1.25 m/s? | Both shed. 0007/100 ties for best in fresh air, so one fin suits every wind. |

The studies so far.

## Reproducing this {.appendix .unnumbered}

Everything is in [the repository](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd): the simulation setup
(`projects/foil2d/`), every study file, and a findings log per study with the numbers behind each
conclusion. Simulations run in Docker (`uv run iomcfd run foil2d/<study>`) or on Google Cloud Batch.
This page is built from `site/` with Quarto; its charts are drawn from the small data files below,
which `iomcfd site export` copies out of the runs. The code is under the
[MIT licence](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/LICENSE); the text, figures and data on
this page are under CC BY 4.0. Reference data from other sources keeps its own terms.
